clinicalPearls: A functional cyst that forms when the corpus luteum fails to involute after ovulation and instead enlarges with fluid or blood
Commonly asymptomatic and self-limiting, but may cause unilateral lower abdominal pain, particularly if it bleeds internally
On ultrasound it often shows a thick, crenated wall with peripheral circumferential blood flow, described as a ring of fire
Haemorrhage into the cyst can produce a lace-like or reticular pattern of internal echoes as the clot organises
The corpus luteum supports early pregnancy, so a luteal cyst is a normal finding in the first trimester
Rupture may cause haemoperitoneum, and right-sided rupture can closely mimic acute appendicitis
Most resolve spontaneously and are managed expectantly, with surgery reserved for significant bleeding or diagnostic uncertainty
reference.pathophysiology: After ovulation the ruptured follicle normally organises into a corpus luteum that regresses if pregnancy does not occur. When involution fails, the corpus luteum persists and accumulates fluid or blood, forming a cyst. Bleeding from the vascular granulosa lining into the cyst cavity distends it and may cause pain; if the wall gives way, blood escapes into the peritoneal cavity. The extent of any resulting haemoperitoneum is greater in women taking anticoagulants or with a bleeding tendency.
additionalInvestigations: Urinary or serum pregnancy test, and serial beta-hCG where ectopic pregnancy must be excluded
Transvaginal ultrasound with Doppler to demonstrate the characteristic peripheral vascular rim
Full blood count if intracystic or intraperitoneal bleeding is suspected
Assessment for free fluid in the pelvis and abdomen when rupture is a concern
Follow-up ultrasound to confirm resolution when the diagnosis is uncertain
redFlags: A positive pregnancy test raising the possibility of ectopic pregnancy
Anticoagulant therapy or a bleeding disorder increasing the risk of severe haemorrhage
reference.prognosis: Corpus luteum cysts are benign and typically resolve spontaneously within one or two menstrual cycles; even after rupture, most women recover well with conservative management, and surgery is only occasionally required.
pitfalls: Mistaking a haemorrhagic corpus luteum for an ectopic pregnancy or vice versa
Underestimating the volume of haemoperitoneum, particularly in anticoagulated patients
Overlooking coexisting ovarian torsion in a woman with a luteal cyst
Proceeding to surgery for a cyst that would have resolved with observation
